title: Development of a Systematic Humor Pedagogical Framework to Enhance Student Learning Outcomes https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666374025000044
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), February 21, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers Ngai et al.'s development of PHISTLE (Planned Humor Incorporation System for Teaching and Learning Enhancement), a framework for systematically building content-related humor into teaching, tested across disciplines in Hong Kong higher education. The research finds that strategic content-related humor — word play, exaggerated descriptions, analogies, anecdotes — enhances engagement, motivation, and creates a more relaxed classroom, while aggressive, offensive, unrelated, other-disparaging, and sarcastic humor should be avoided entirely. The study is specific about dosage: three to four content-related jokes per lesson is optimal, with too much diverting attention from the material itself. When humor precedes a topic, the framework recommends a deliberate 'Point of Return to Reality' to signal the joke has ended and refocus students, and throughout, teachers are cautioned to keep humor in balance with professionalism so as not to undermine their credibility.
points: Effectiveness depends on how humor is used, not simply whether it's used — content-related word play, analogies, and anecdotes work; sarcastic, disparaging, or unrelated humor does not.
There's a specific optimal dosage: three to four content-related humor instances per roughly 50 minutes of lesson; more than that risks diverting attention away from the material.
When humor is used before introducing a topic, a deliberate “Point of Return to Reality” should signal the joke's end so students don't stay confused about what's serious content.
Teachers need to balance humor with professionalism — used carelessly, humor can undermine classroom credibility even as it's meant to build engagement.
quotes: It is not simply the use of humor, but how humor is used, that determines its effectiveness in the classroom

Specific types of content-related humor are effective, such as word play, exaggerated/absurd descriptions, analogies, and anecdotes. Aggressive, offensive, unrelated, other-disparaging, and sarcastic humor should be avoided.
Three to four jokes or instances of content-related humor per lesson are optimal, as too much humor may divert students' attention.
When using pre-topic incorporation, a "Point of Return to Reality" (PRR) should be included to signal the end of the joke and avoid confusion.
There should be a balance between humor and professionalism. Teachers should be judicious in their use of humor to maintain credibility in the classroom.
